notes:
I couldn't find much on two of your three areas. Protestant traditions don't really disagree about this psalm, apart from one difference on v. 6. I found nothing from Orthodox sources or on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching. One of my searches also failed to pull up NET Bible notes or Wesley's Notes, so neither is used below.

The church labels in brackets come from my general knowledge, not from the pages.

---

## Title and setting

- **Two betrayals:** The Ziphites betrayed David twice (1 Samuel 23 and 26). Guzik thinks the psalm fits 1 Samuel 23 best: David knew he had been betrayed, but God had not yet rescued him. There were actually two times when the Ziphites betrayed David unto King Saul, first in 1 Samuel 23 and the second in 1 Samuel 26. David escaped both times, but the circumstances of this psalm seem to best fit the circumstances of 1 Samuel 23. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/
- **"Maskil":** Guzik cites Boice that the word might be better understood as *instruction*. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/
- **Henry:** He calls the Ziphites, men of Judah (types of Judas the traitor). https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_054.cfm
- **Coffman:** He explains that Abiathar, a priest who brought the ephod, warned David by God's word to leave first Keilah and then Ziph. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-54.html
- **Catholic (Augustine):** He reads Saul as a picture of an earthly kingdom headed for death, and David as bearing the figure of Christ, or of the Body of Christ. He takes "Ziphites" to mean "men flourishing": the worldly who do well now, while Christ's people are "hidden" (Col 3:3). https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801054.htm

## v. 1

- **"By Your name":** God's name stands for his character; his "might" stands for his power. Guzik quotes Maclaren that nothing less than the whole fulness of the manifested God is enough for the necessities of one poor man. Guzik adds that David's rescue would also prove him in the right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/
- **Gill (Baptist):** God answered this prayer in a remarkable way. Saul had to break off the chase to fight the Philistines (1 Sam 23:26), and later David spared Saul's life (1 Sam 26). Gill also applies the verse to Christ, and to sinners who ask God to save them through his Son. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-1.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** "Name" stands for God's power, goodness and truth. "Judge me" means "vindicate me." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-1.htm
- **Calvin (Reformed):** By asking God to judge him, David is claiming his cause is right. Anyone asking for God's protection must first be sure their cause is good. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-54.html
- **Keil and Delitzsch:** God's name shows his nature, and mercy is at its centre. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-1.htm
- **Augustine:** "Judge me" would sound like a curse unless God first saves us by his name. For those he has saved, his judgment separates them from the wicked rather than punishing them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801054.htm

## v. 2

- **Guzik:** Asking God to "hear" was a normal prayer. It was assumed that if God heard, he would act. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/
- **Spurgeon (Baptist):** Hear my prayer, which comes from my heart (that line is Henry's). Spurgeon calls prayer the one weapon an enemy can't disable, and says praying out loud helps keep the mind awake. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-1.htm
- **Calvin:** David isn't telling God something he doesn't know. He is unloading his own fears. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-54.html
- **Augustine:** He uses the verse to teach that God sometimes refuses earthly requests for our good. Don't tell the doctor which medicine to prescribe. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801054.htm

## v. 3

- **Why "strangers," when the Ziphites were fellow Judahites?** The commentators answer differently:
  - **Most:** It describes how they acted. They were countrymen who behaved like foreigners (Guzik, quoting Horne). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/ Henry calls them unworthy the name of Israelites. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/psalms-54.html
  - **Coke:** Perhaps Ziph's people really were mostly foreigners living under Israel's rule. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/psalms-54.html
  - **Coffman:** He calls them pagans. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-54.html
  - **Augustine:** They were foreign "not in tribe… but in flower," meaning in their worldliness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801054.htm
- **Text and translation:** The editor's note in Calvin's commentary says more than twenty manuscripts read "the proud" instead of "strangers," as the Aramaic paraphrase does. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/psalms-54.html Spurgeon's Treasury quotes a writer who argues the word should be "spies." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm Constable notes the verse is almost the same as Psalm 86:14. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-54.html
- **"No regard for God":** Spurgeon says David felt that atheism lay at the bottom of the enmity which pursued him. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm
- **"Selah":** Spurgeon takes it as a pause for breath, and says our own prayers would gain from more pauses. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-1.htm

## v. 4

- **The key debate.** The Hebrew literally says "the Lord is among those who uphold my life." Readers take it two ways:
  - **God works through human helpers.** Guzik quotes Kidner: the old translations found the Hebrew startling, but it means seeing His hand behind the human help. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/ Calvin thinks of Jonathan and others who cared for David. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/54-4.html
  - **God is the one Upholder.** Keil and Delitzsch say God isn't one helper among many but fills the whole category himself. The Cambridge Bible and the Pulpit Commentary say much the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-4.htm
  - **Henry combines both:** God is the chief helper, and none of the others could help unless he helped them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/54-4.html
  - **Clarke:** It may even mean the Philistines, whose raid made Saul turn back. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-54.html
- **"Behold":** Maclaren pictures David standing up from prayer and pointing his enemies to his Helper (via Guzik). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/ Spurgeon pictures "Adonai" in the camp of David's defenders. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm
- **Augustine:** God is a sweet help today, in the heart, even while his promises are still far off. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.LIV.html

## v. 5

- **Praying against enemies:**
  - **Guzik:** David prayed for God to cut them off, but wouldn't take revenge himself. He spared Saul's life in 1 Samuel 26 and waited for God. Guzik admits Jesus taught a more generous prayer for enemies (Matt 5:44), but says wanting good to win is still right. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/
  - **Constable**, quoting another writer: "The imprecation is not vindictive but expressive of trust in divine justice." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/psalms-54.html
- **"In Your faithfulness" (or "truth"):**
  - **Clarke** (via Guzik): God's truth is pledged to keep his promises to David, so it requires that the enemies be cut off. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/
  - **Henry:** God keeps his threats as well as his promises. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-4.htm
  - **Keil:** God's truth is the reason the enemies are cut off, not the tool that does it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-6.htm
- **The Hebrew text:** In this verse, the word for "enemies" can mean "those who watch me." Coke says the Ziphites were spying for Saul. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tcc/psalms-54.html Keil discusses a textual variant that reads "evil shall return on my spies." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-7.htm
- **Coffman:** He rejects the idea that God never really punishes anyone. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-54.html

## v. 6

- **The common reading:** This is a freewill offering, given out of gratitude rather than because the Law required it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/ Constable thinks it would have been a peace (fellowship) offering. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/54-6.html
- **Where traditions differ: was it a real animal sacrifice?**
  - **Calvin (Reformed):** David also meant to give thanks with the rituals the Law prescribed. Although God looks mainly at the heart, that doesn't excuse skipping the rites. "Freely" means cheerfully, not "optional." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/54-6.html
  - **Gill (Baptist):** "Not legal sacrifices," but praise from his mouth. Gill applies it to Christ's willing self-offering, and to believers' prayers, praise and good works. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-6.htm
  - **Keil and Delitzsch (Lutheran scholars):** The sacrifices are ritual, but as an outward sign of the spiritual. They are not "spiritual sacrifices" set against ritual ones. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-6.htm
  - **Henry:** The sacrifice was only the shadow; the substance is a thankful heart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/54-6.html
- **"For it is good":** Spurgeon reads it two ways: God's name is good, and so is praising it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm
- **A vow?** Maclaren says this isn't a bargaining vow ("I'll give if you hear me"). It is glad anticipation by someone who knows he's been heard. https://biblehub.com/sermons/psalms/54-6.htm
- **"O LORD":** Bible.org notes that God's covenant name, YHWH, is rare in this part of the Psalms. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-54

## v. 7

- **Past tense, future meaning:** "He has delivered" is faith speaking about a rescue still to come. Guzik quotes Trapp: "the triumph of trust." He links the verse to Saul being called away by the Philistine raid (1 Sam 23:27–28). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/ Ellicott translates it "when he shall have delivered." https://biblehub.com/psalms/54-7.htm
- **"Stared down my foes":** The words "his desire" (KJV) are not in the Hebrew. Commentators fill the gap differently:
  - **Clarke:** "My eye has seen my enemies" — they came close but were kept away. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/54-7.html
  - **Davidson** (in Spurgeon's Treasury): David could face them without fear. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm
  - **Henry:** He didn't see them destroyed, only forced to retreat. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_054.cfm
  - **Augustine:** David looks back from God's height and sees that "all flesh is grass." https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf108.ii.LIV.html
- **Is it gloating?**
  - **Barnes:** This is not the expression of malice, but of certainty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-7.htm
  - **Spurgeon and Gill:** David rejoiced in God's justice, not personal spite. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm
  - **Cambridge Bible:** Such rejoicing over the fall of enemies is not of the spirit of the Gospel. But it says the real motive is far above a thirst for revenge. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/54-7.htm
  - **A sharper modern view:** Coffman reports that J.M.P. Smith translated the line "my eye has gloated over my foes" and called it a "nasty note of personal vengeance." Coffman rejects this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/psalms-54.html
- **Reading the psalm as about Christ:** Guzik hears the psalm in Jesus' mouth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-54/ Spurgeon's Treasury quotes a writer noting that the church appointed this psalm to remember Christ's passion. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps054.cfm
